title: Pray and work
hook: the Rule of Benedict gives monks set hours for prayer, work and reading (Rule of Benedict 48)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tentmaker: Paul at a bench in Corinth, paying his own way. Your line was work with my hands. What did your hands take back? Day eight hundred ninety.

A bell rings in a monastery. Somewhere a monk sets down a hoe at the edge of a vegetable bed, wipes his hands, and walks to the chapel. Later another bell, and he'll walk back to the garden, or to the kitchen, or to a desk with a book open on it. The day isn't one long prayer, and it isn't one long shift. It's divided, on purpose, into pieces. The plan for that day comes from a book written for monks, the Rule of Saint Benedict. Later readers summed up its way of life in a Latin motto. Today's word.
screen: `A BELL IN THE GARDEN.` → `A DAY IN PIECES, ON PURPOSE.` → `A LATIN MOTTO.`

segments.voice: Ora et labora. Pray and work. First, those words aren't in the Rule itself. The Rule has its own words, and its chapter on daily work opens with a blunt sentence: idleness is the enemy of the soul. So, it says, the brothers should be busy at set times with the work of their hands, and at other set hours with holy reading. The times shift with the seasons, and between them come the hours of prayer the community keeps together. Second, what the work is for. The Rule says that when monks live by the labor of their hands, as the apostles did, then they are truly monks. Work isn't what they do when prayer is over. It's part of the same life. If the harvest needs them, they're told not to be upset about going out to gather it. Third, room for the weak. Benedict thinks about the weak brother as well as the strong one. Those who are sick or delicate, the Rule says, should get work suited to them, so they're neither idle nor crushed by it and driven away. Fourth, why it reaches past the monastery. Benedictine monks and nuns still live by this Rule, and some people outside any monastery borrow its shape for their own days. The insight is simple and practical: when prayer, work and reading each have their own time, none of them swallows the others. The work gets done. The prayer doesn't get skipped. And the mind gets fed. A day in three, kept on purpose.
screen: `THE MOTTO ISN'T IN THE RULE.` · `IDLENESS, THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.` · `WORK SUITED TO THE WEAK.` · `A DAY IN THREE, ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `ORA ET LABORA.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath slow. Now walk through the rest of your day in your mind, from this moment to sleep. Find three small places in it. One for work, the thing that most needs your hands. One for prayer or stillness, even five minutes, whatever that means for you. One for reading, a page of something that feeds you. Give each one a rough time. Then let the plan go, and just sit, the way a monk might between bells. If you pray, you can use these two minutes as the first of the three. The bell holds the time.
Ora et labora. Latin for pray and work: the motto later readers gave to Benedict's Rule, which gives monks set hours for prayer, work and reading. Today's word.
Your line: pray and work. Today, divide your day into three: a block for work, a block for stillness or prayer, a block for reading. Keep them, even if they're small. Day eight hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Benedict, keeping set hours of prayer together and set times for work and holy reading; some lay people, called oblates, follow the Rule's shape in ordinary life.

fork.setup: you're a monk, and the harvest is ready but the community is short of hands. the Rule's hours say it's time for reading. what does the Rule say?
options: stay at your reading, the hours are fixed.
go out and gather the harvest, without being upset about it.
pay workers so the monks can keep praying.
fork.reveal: the Rule says if need requires them to gather the harvest themselves, they shouldn't be distressed: living by their own labor is part of being truly monks.

original.note: Latin, from the Christian monastic tradition: pray and work, a later motto for the Rule of Benedict.
